questions.question: How do you solve problems with arrays and hashes in Ruby?
questions.title: Solving Array and Hash Problems
questions.direct_answer: Arrays (ordered, indexed) and hashes (key-value) are the two workhorses of Ruby DSA. Common patterns: use a hash as a frequency map (count chars/elements: str.chars.tally), use two pointers on a sorted array (see from both ends), use a hash for O(1) lookups (seen[x] to find a pair sum), use sliding window for subarrays (max sum of k consecutive). The key is picking the structure for the operation: hash for lookup/count, array for order/index, and using Enumerable (map/select/reduce/tally) to write the loop concisely.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you use a hash as a frequency map / O(1) lookup and know the patterns (two pointers, sliding window) and Enumerable helpers (tally).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an O(n) array search where a hash gives O(1), or nested loops (O(n^2)) where a hash makes it O(n).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a hash as a frequency map (tally) or O(1) lookup (seen[x]); arrays for order/index. Patterns: two pointers, sliding window. Enumerable writes it concisely.

sections.title: Two Workhorses and Their Patterns
sections.content: Arrays (ordered, indexed) and hashes (key-value) are the two workhorses of Ruby DSA. Common patterns: use a hash as a frequency map (count characters or elements with str.chars.tally), use two pointers on a sorted array (walk from both ends toward the middle), use a hash for O(1) lookups (a seen[x] hash to find a pair that sums to a target), and use a sliding window for subarray problems (the max sum of k consecutive elements). The key is picking the structure for the operation you need: a hash for lookup or counting, an array for order and index, and using Enumerable methods like map, select, reduce, and tally to write the loop concisely rather than with an index variable.

sections.title: Hash for Lookup/Count, Array for Order
sections.content:
A hash gives O(1) lookup/count; an array gives order/index.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[problem] -->|count or lookup| H[hash: tally, seen]
  P -->|order or window| A[array: two pointers, sliding window]
```

sections.title: Array & hash patterns
sections.content:
```ruby
# Frequency map: count characters
str = 'hello'
str.chars.tally                   # {'h'=>1, 'e'=>1, 'l'=>2, 'o'=>1}

# O(1) lookup: two-sum (find a pair that sums to target)
def two_sum(nums, target)
  seen = {}
  nums.each do |n|
    return [seen[target - n], n] if seen.key?(target - n)
    seen[n] = n
  end
  nil
end

# Two pointers on a sorted array (pair sum)
def two_sorted(nums, target)
  lo, hi = 0, nums.length - 1
  while lo < hi
    s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
    return [nums[lo], nums[hi]] if s == target
    s < target ? lo += 1 : hi -= 1
  end
end

# Sliding window: max sum of k consecutive
def max_sum(nums, k)
  win = nums.first(k).sum
  best = win
  (k...nums.length).each do |i|
    win += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
    best = [best, win].max
  end
  best
end
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using O(n) array include?/index where a hash gives O(1) lookup.
Nested loops (O(n^2)) for pair problems where a hash makes it O(n).
Forgetting Enumerable helpers (tally, sum, each_cons) that write the loop concisely.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Arrays (order/index) and hashes (key/value) are the two workhorses of Ruby DSA.
Use a hash as a frequency map (tally) or for O(1) lookup (seen[x]).
Two pointers: walk a sorted array from both ends (pair problems).
Sliding window: track a k-width window for subarray max/min/sum.
Enumerable (tally, sum, each_cons) writes the loop concisely — use it.
